claim: Resting-state fMRI studies have provided a broad picture of the connectivity between human neocortex and cerebellum.
source: While resting-state fMRI studies have provided a broad picture of the connectivity between human neocortex and cerebellum, the degree of convergence of cortical inputs onto cerebellar circuits remains unknown.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, drawing on established knowledge from prior resting-state fMRI research.

claim: The degree of convergence of cortical inputs onto cerebellar circuits remains unknown.
source: While resting-state fMRI studies have provided a broad picture of the connectivity between human neocortex and cerebellum, the degree of convergence of cortical inputs onto cerebellar circuits remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge, based on inference from the existing literature.

claim: Models that allow some degree of convergence provided the best predictions of cerebellar activity patterns.
source: We compared these models by their ability to predict cerebellar activity patterns for novel Task Sets. Models that allow some degree of convergence provided the best predictions, arguing for convergence of multiple cortical inputs onto single cerebellar voxels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from model comparisons presented in the study.

claim: Multiple cortical inputs converge onto single cerebellar voxels.
source: Models that allow some degree of convergence provided the best predictions, arguing for convergence of multiple cortical inputs onto single cerebellar voxels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the superior performance of convergent models in predicting cerebellar activity.

claim: The degree of convergence varied across the cerebellum.
source: Importantly, the degree of convergence varied across the cerebellum with the highest convergence observed in areas linked to language, working memory, and social cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing regional variation in convergence measures.

claim: The highest convergence was observed in cerebellar areas linked to language, working memory, and social cognition.
source: Importantly, the degree of convergence varied across the cerebellum with the highest convergence observed in areas linked to language, working memory, and social cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing higher convergence in specific functional regions of the cerebellum.

claim: There are important differences in the way that functional subdivisions of the cerebellum support motor and cognitive function.
source: These findings suggest important differences in the way that functional subdivisions of the cerebellum support motor and cognitive function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed variation in convergence patterns across motor and cognitive cerebellar regions.

claim: Cerebellar activation in a semantic retrieval task was first reported by Petersen et al., 1989.
source: Since the first report of cerebellar activation in a semantic retrieval task (Petersen et al., 1989), thousands of neuroimaging papers have reported cerebellar recruitment during a broad range of tasks that cannot be attributed to the motor demands of these tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Thousands of neuroimaging papers have reported cerebellar recruitment during a broad range of tasks that cannot be attributed to the motor demands of these tasks.
source: Since the first report of cerebellar activation in a semantic retrieval task (Petersen et al., 1989), thousands of neuroimaging papers have reported cerebellar recruitment during a broad range of tasks that cannot be attributed to the motor demands of these tasks.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, drawing on established knowledge from the neuroimaging literature.

claim: The cerebellum may facilitate attentional shifts.
source: Functional interpretations include hypotheses concerning how the cerebellum may facilitate attentional shifts (Allen et al., 1997), stimulus-response mapping (Bischoff-Grethe et al., 2002), higher order rule processing (Balsters et al., 2013), verbal working memory (Marvel and Desmond, 2010), language (Fiez, 2016), and social cognition (Van Overwalle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Allen et al., 1997.

claim: The cerebellum may facilitate stimulus-response mapping.
source: Functional interpretations include hypotheses concerning how the cerebellum may facilitate attentional shifts (Allen et al., 1997), stimulus-response mapping (Bischoff-Grethe et al., 2002), higher order rule processing (Balsters et al., 2013), verbal working memory (Marvel and Desmond, 2010), language (Fiez, 2016), and social cognition (Van Overwalle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bischoff-Grethe et al., 2002.

claim: The cerebellum may facilitate higher order rule processing.
source: Functional interpretations include hypotheses concerning how the cerebellum may facilitate attentional shifts (Allen et al., 1997), stimulus-response mapping (Bischoff-Grethe et al., 2002), higher order rule processing (Balsters et al., 2013), verbal working memory (Marvel and Desmond, 2010), language (Fiez, 2016), and social cognition (Van Overwalle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Balsters et al., 2013.

claim: The cerebellum may facilitate verbal working memory.
source: Functional interpretations include hypotheses concerning how the cerebellum may facilitate attentional shifts (Allen et al., 1997), stimulus-response mapping (Bischoff-Grethe et al., 2002), higher order rule processing (Balsters et al., 2013), verbal working memory (Marvel and Desmond, 2010), language (Fiez, 2016), and social cognition (Van Overwalle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marvel and Desmond, 2010.

claim: The cerebellum may facilitate language.
source: Functional interpretations include hypotheses concerning how the cerebellum may facilitate attentional shifts (Allen et al., 1997), stimulus-response mapping (Bischoff-Grethe et al., 2002), higher order rule processing (Balsters et al., 2013), verbal working memory (Marvel and Desmond, 2010), language (Fiez, 2016), and social cognition (Van Overwalle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fiez, 2016.

claim: The cerebellum may facilitate social cognition.
source: Functional interpretations include hypotheses concerning how the cerebellum may facilitate attentional shifts (Allen et al., 1997), stimulus-response mapping (Bischoff-Grethe et al., 2002), higher order rule processing (Balsters et al., 2013), verbal working memory (Marvel and Desmond, 2010), language (Fiez, 2016), and social cognition (Van Overwalle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Van Overwalle et al., 2015.

claim: Functional maps of the cerebellum depict the association of particular cognitive processes with different subregions of the cerebellum.
source: This body of work has produced functional maps of the cerebellum that depict the association of particular cognitive processes with different subregions of the cerebellum (King et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to King et al., 2019.

claim: Differences in cerebellar function mainly arise from variation in the input to the cerebellum.
source: Given the relative uniform cytoarchitecture of the cerebellar cortex, it is assumed that differences in function mainly arise from variation in the input to the cerebellum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known uniform cytoarchitecture of the cerebellar cortex.

claim: The cerebellar cortex has relatively uniform cytoarchitecture.
source: Given the relative uniform cytoarchitecture of the cerebellar cortex, it is assumed that differences in function mainly arise from variation in the input to the cerebellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Trans-synaptic tracing methods in non-human primates have revealed extensive reciprocal connections between many frontal and parietal areas and the cerebellum.
source: Trans-synaptic tracing methods employed in non-human primates studies have revealed extensive reciprocal connections between many frontal and parietal areas and the cerebellum (Dum and Strick, 2003; Kelly and Strick, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dum and Strick, 2003 and Kelly and Strick, 2003.

claim: Cortico-cerebellar connections are closed-loop in nature, with each cortical region projecting to a specific cerebellar region and receiving input from the same area.
source: These studies have highlighted the closed-loop nature of these connections, with each (neo-)cortical region projecting to a specific cerebellar region, and receiving input from the same area (Strick et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Strick et al., 2009.

claim: Resting state functional connectivity analyses have revealed a set of cerebellar networks, each one associated with a specific cortical network.
source: In humans, resting state functional connectivity analyses have revealed a set of cerebellar networks, each one associated with a specific cortical network (Buckner et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2019; Marek et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buckner et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2019; and Marek et al., 2018.

claim: Recent work in the rodent brain has suggested convergence of mossy fibers from diverse sources onto the same cerebellar region.
source: Indeed, recent work in the rodent brain has suggested convergence of mossy fibers from diverse sources onto the same cerebellar region (Henschke and Pakan, 2020; Pisano et al., 2021), or even onto the same granule cells (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henschke and Pakan, 2020 and Pisano et al., 2021.

claim: Mossy fibers from diverse sources can converge onto the same granule cells.
source: Indeed, recent work in the rodent brain has suggested convergence of mossy fibers from diverse sources onto the same cerebellar region (Henschke and Pakan, 2020; Pisano et al., 2021), or even onto the same granule cells (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2013.

claim: Cortical areas show considerable variation in the degree to which they serve as points of convergence from other cortical regions.
source: Furthermore, the pattern of cortico-cerebellar convergence may vary across the cerebellar cortex, similar to how cortical areas show considerable variation in the degree to which they serve as points of convergence from other cortical regions (Bertolero et al., 2015; Yeo et al., 2014; Yeo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bertolero et al., 2015; Yeo et al., 2014; and Yeo et al., 2015.

claim: The BOLD signal in the cerebellar cortex overwhelmingly reflects cortical input via the pons.
source: The BOLD signal in the cerebellar cortex overwhelmingly reflects cortical input (via the pons) with no measurable contribution from the Purkinje cells, the output neurons of the cerebellar cortex (Mathiesen et al., 2000; Thomsen et al., 2004; Alahmadi et al., 2016; Alahmadi et al., 2015; Mapelli et al., 2017; Gagliano et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mathiesen et al., 2000; Thomsen et al., 2004; Alahmadi et al., 2016; Alahmadi et al., 2015; Mapelli et al., 2017; and Gagliano et al., 2022.

claim: Purkinje cells make no measurable contribution to the BOLD signal in the cerebellar cortex.
source: The BOLD signal in the cerebellar cortex overwhelmingly reflects cortical input (via the pons) with no measurable contribution from the Purkinje cells, the output neurons of the cerebellar cortex (Mathiesen et al., 2000; Thomsen et al., 2004; Alahmadi et al., 2016; Alahmadi et al., 2015; Mapelli et al., 2017; Gagliano et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mathiesen et al., 2000; Thomsen et al., 2004; Alahmadi et al., 2016; Alahmadi et al., 2015; Mapelli et al., 2017; and Gagliano et al., 2022.

claim: Purkinje cells are the output neurons of the cerebellar cortex.
source: The BOLD signal in the cerebellar cortex overwhelmingly reflects cortical input (via the pons) with no measurable contribution from the Purkinje cells, the output neurons of the cerebellar cortex (Mathiesen et al., 2000; Thomsen et al., 2004; Alahmadi et al., 2016; Alahmadi et al., 2015; Mapelli et al., 2017; Gagliano et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: The neocortical BOLD signal reflects many sources including inputs from other cortical regions, local activity, and ascending input.
source: In contrast, the neocortical BOLD signal reflects many sources including inputs from other cortical regions, local activity (input and output), as well as ascending input.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sources contributing to the neocortical BOLD signal.

claim: Cerebellar input via the thalamus makes a relatively small contribution to the overall BOLD response in the neocortex.
source: While the latter will include cerebellar input via the thalamus, this source is likely to make a relatively small contribution to the overall BOLD response in the neocortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the multiple sources contributing to the neocortical BOLD signal.

claim: The relationship between neocortical and cerebellar BOLD signals is most informative in evaluating cortico-cerebellar connectivity.
source: As such, the relationship between neocortical and cerebellar BOLD signals will be most informative in evaluating cortico-cerebellar connectivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential contributions to BOLD signals in the two structures.

claim: The multi-domain task battery was designed to engage cognitive processes across a broad range of functional domains.
source: We trained multiple models of neocortical-cerebellar connectivity on a fMRI data set obtained while human participants completed a large task battery that was designed to engage cognitive processes across a broad range of functional domains (e.g. visual cognition, memory, attention, cognitive control).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Ridge models outperformed WTA models in predicting cerebellar activity.
source: Averaged across all levels of granularity, the Ridge models outperformed the WTA models (F1,23 = 47.122, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The advantage of Ridge models over WTA models was consistent across all levels of granularity starting with a parcellation of 80 regions.
source: Post-hoc tests revealed that this advantage for the Ridge model was consistent across all levels of granularity, starting with a parcellation of 80 regions (t23=5.172, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical tests of the experimental data.

claim: There was a significant difference in predictive accuracy between the Ridge and Lasso models.
source: We also found a significant difference in predictive accuracy between the Ridge and Lasso model (F1,23 = 15.055, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in predictive accuracy between Ridge and Lasso models at the lowest level of granularity.
source: Post-hoc tests showed that there was no significant difference in predictive accuracy at the lowest level of granularity (t23=1.279, p=0.213), whereas the difference was significant for the finer parcellations (all t23 >10.937, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical tests of the experimental data.

claim: The difference in predictive accuracy between Ridge and Lasso models was significant for finer parcellations.
source: Post-hoc tests showed that there was no significant difference in predictive accuracy at the lowest level of granularity (t23=1.279, p=0.213), whereas the difference was significant for the finer parcellations (all t23 >10.937, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical tests of the experimental data.

claim: The mean predictive accuracy of the Lasso and Ridge models was 0.257.
source: The mean predictive accuracy of the Lasso and Ridge models was 0.257 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The correlation of the measured cerebellar activity patterns across the two sessions of Task Set B was, on average, r=0.51.
source: The correlation of the measured cerebellar activity patterns across the two sessions of Task Set B was, on average, r=0.51 (SD = 0.102).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data measuring inter-session reliability.

claim: Reliability of cerebellar activity was fairly consistent across the cerebellum.
source: Reliability was fairly consistent across the cerebellum (Figure 2C), with some decreases in lobules I-IV.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The decrease in reliability in lobules I-IV likely reflects the fact that the task battery only included hand and eye movements and did not activate the lower body representation.
source: This dropoff likely reflects the fact that our battery only included hand and eye movements, and did not activate the lower body representation that is prominent in this area.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known somatotopic organization of the cerebellum and the task design.

claim: The Ridge model was able to predict approximately 45% of the systematic variance of the cerebellar activity patterns across tasks.
source: Overall, the noise ceiling calculation showed that the Ridge model was able to predict approximately 45% of the systematic variance of the cerebellar activity patterns across tasks (average R2=0.672).
evidence: This claim is supported by the noise ceiling calculation applied to the experimental data.

claim: Predictive accuracy was best in anterior motor regions of the cerebellum.
source: While the predictive accuracy (Figure 2D) was best in anterior motor regions, it was reasonably high across the entire cerebellar surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Predictive accuracy was reasonably high across the entire cerebellar surface.
source: While the predictive accuracy (Figure 2D) was best in anterior motor regions, it was reasonably high across the entire cerebellar surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The connectivity model predicted the pattern of task activity with a high degree of fidelity for spatial working memory and social cognition tasks.
source: The predicted and observed activity patterns for two exemplary tasks (Figure 2E) demonstrate the quality of these predictions at the group level. In both of these examples, (spatial working memory and social cognition tasks), the connectivity model predicted the pattern of task activity with a high degree of fidelity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The training set did not include a task with similar characteristics to the spatial working memory task.
source: This is especially compelling for the spatial working memory task as the training set did not include a task with similar characteristics.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Using a 7-network cortical parcellation, the WTA model was inferior to the Ridge models.
source: For example, we used a 7-network cortical parcellation based on resting state fMRI data (Yeo et al., 2011) to train and test the three models. Here, too, the WTA model was inferior to the Ridge models (t23=2.956, p<0.01), with no performance difference between Ridge and Lasso models (t23=–1.235, p=0.229).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data using an alternative parcellation.

claim: There was no performance difference between Ridge and Lasso models when using a 7-network cortical parcellation.
source: For example, we used a 7-network cortical parcellation based on resting state fMRI data (Yeo et al., 2011) to train and test the three models. Here, too, the WTA model was inferior to the Ridge models (t23=2.956, p<0.01), with no performance difference between Ridge and Lasso models (t23=–1.235, p=0.229).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data using an alternative parcellation.

claim: The pattern of WTA model inferiority held when using other common functional parcellations of the neocortex.
source: The same pattern held when we used other common functional parcellations of the neocortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Models which entail some degree of convergence from the neocortex to the cerebellum outperform a model in which cerebellar activity is based on input from a single cortical region.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that models which entail some degree of convergence from the neocortex to the cerebellum outperform a model in which cerebellar activity is based on input from a single cortical region.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The conclusion about convergence holds across a broad range of cortical parcellations.
source: This conclusion holds across a broad range of cortical parcellations (Zhi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhi et al., 2022 and the data from multiple parcellations.

claim: The input to the hand regions of the cerebellum (regions 1 and 2) was centered around the contralateral primary sensorimotor cortex with some additional input from premotor and parietal cortex.
source: As expected given the crossed connectivity between M1 and lobules IV/V (Kelly and Strick, 2003; Krienen and Buckner, 2009; O'Reilly et al., 2010), the input to the hand regions of the cerebellum (regions 1 and 2) was centered around the contralateral primary sensorimotor cortex with some additional input from premotor and parietal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to Kelly and Strick, 2003; Krienen and Buckner, 2009; and O'Reilly et al., 2010.

claim: There is crossed connectivity between M1 and lobules IV/V.
source: As expected given the crossed connectivity between M1 and lobules IV/V (Kelly and Strick, 2003; Krienen and Buckner, 2009; O'Reilly et al., 2010), the input to the hand regions of the cerebellum (regions 1 and 2) was centered around the contralateral primary sensorimotor cortex with some additional input from premotor and parietal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kelly and Strick, 2003; Krienen and Buckner, 2009; and O'Reilly et al., 2010.

claim: Activity in region 3, the oculomotor vermis, is predicted by a bilateral set of cortical regions including the frontal eye fields, regions in the intraparietal sulcus, and extrastriate visual regions.
source: Activity in region 3, the oculomotor vermis, is predicted by a bilateral set of cortical regions including the frontal eye fields (FEF), regions in the intraparietal sulcus, and extrastriate visual regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the connectivity model.

claim: Region 4, an area strongly activated during action observation, is predicted by a bilateral network of regions including premotor cortex, supplementary motor cortex and parietal cortex.
source: Region 4, an area strongly activated during action observation, is predicted by a bilateral network of regions including premotor cortex, supplementary motor cortex (SMA) and parietal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the connectivity model.

claim: Cerebellar regions 5–10, the regions associated with more cognitive processes, are predicted by a distributed set of cortical regions, with stronger input coming from the contralateral cortical hemisphere.
source: Cerebellar regions 5–10, the regions associated with more cognitive processes are predicted by a distributed set of cortical regions, with stronger input coming from the contralateral cortical hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the connectivity model.

claim: Cerebellar region 5, a region restricted to the left cerebellum, receives much stronger input from the right cerebral hemisphere.
source: For example, cerebellar region 5, a region restricted to the left cerebellum, receives much stronger input from the right cerebral hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the connectivity model.

claim: Most cerebellar regions are best predicted by multiple cortical regions.
source: In summary, these results suggest that most cerebellar regions are best predicted by multiple cortical regions, pointing to some degree of cortical-cerebellar convergence.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Inputs to hand motor regions MDTB (regions 1 and 2) arise from a relatively small area of the neocortex.
source: For example, inputs to hand motor regions MDTB (regions 1 and 2) arise from a relatively small area of the neocortex, while inputs to regions in lobule VII (regions 3–10) come from a larger area.
evidence: This is an inference from visual inspection of the connectivity patterns, supported by the data.

claim: Inputs to regions in lobule VII (regions 3–10) come from a larger area of the neocortex.
source: For example, inputs to hand motor regions MDTB (regions 1 and 2) arise from a relatively small area of the neocortex, while inputs to regions in lobule VII (regions 3–10) come from a larger area.
evidence: This is an inference from visual inspection of the connectivity patterns, supported by the data.

claim: Predicting the activity pattern of voxels within Crus I required inclusion of up to 10% of the cortical surface.
source: For example, predicting the activity pattern of voxels within Crus I required inclusion of up to 10% of the cortical surface whereas predicting the activity of voxels in the anterior lobe required less than 5% of the neocortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the Lasso model analysis.

claim: Predicting the activity of voxels in the anterior lobe required less than 5% of the neocortex.
source: For example, predicting the activity pattern of voxels within Crus I required inclusion of up to 10% of the cortical surface whereas predicting the activity of voxels in the anterior lobe required less than 5% of the neocortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the Lasso model analysis.

claim: The size of the estimated cortical input area differed across functional regions of the cerebellum.
source: This analysis confirmed that the size of the estimated cortical input area differed across functional regions (F9,207 = 7.244, p<0.001, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The lowest level of convergence was observed for regions 1 and 2, the anterior hand regions of the cerebellum.
source: The lowest level of convergence was observed for regions 1 and 2, the anterior hand regions of the cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the convergence analysis.

claim: The highest levels of convergence were found in regions of the cerebellum associated with more cognitive functions (e.g. regions 7 and 8, areas engaged during language comprehension).
source: The highest levels of convergence were found in regions of the cerebellum associated with more cognitive functions (e.g. regions 7 and 8, areas engaged during language comprehension).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the convergence analysis.

claim: The pattern of convergence variation holds for cortical parcellations of different levels of granularity.
source: Noteworthy, this pattern holds for cortical parcellations of different levels of granularity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), as well as for the thresholded coefficients from the Ridge regression models (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The observed variation in convergence cannot be explained by the collinearity between different cortical input regions.
source: In this simulation, we did not find any differences in the area of estimated input across cerebellar regions (F9,207=1.762, p=0.076). Thus, the observed variation in convergence cannot be explained by the collinearity between different cortical input regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation data showing no differences in input area when using simulated data with one-to-one connectivity.

claim: The cortical inputs to the hand motor regions of the cerebellum were more concentrated.
source: This analysis revealed a similar pattern as seen in the surface area measure (Figure 4C, D F9,207=18.322, p<0.001). For example, the cortical inputs to the hand motor regions of the cerebellum were more concentrated, whereas the cortical inputs to lobule VII were more dispersed.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dispersion analysis shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: The cortical inputs to lobule VII were more dispersed.
source: This analysis revealed a similar pattern as seen in the surface area measure (Figure 4C, D F9,207=18.322, p<0.001). For example, the cortical inputs to the hand motor regions of the cerebellum were more concentrated, whereas the cortical inputs to lobule VII were more dispersed.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dispersion analysis shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: Cerebellar motor areas such as the hand region in lobule V and VIII received relatively focal cortical input.
source: In summary, we observed variation in the degree of cortico-cerebellar convergence across the cerebellar cortex. In particular, cerebellar motor areas such as the hand region in lobule V and VIII received relatively focal cortical input whereas cerebellar areas associated with cognitive processes (e.g. language, working memory) in lobule VII exhibited a higher degree of convergence.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Cerebellar areas associated with cognitive processes (e.g. language, working memory) in lobule VII exhibited a higher degree of convergence.
source: In summary, we observed variation in the degree of cortico-cerebellar convergence across the cerebellar cortex. In particular, cerebellar motor areas such as the hand region in lobule V and VIII received relatively focal cortical input whereas cerebellar areas associated with cognitive processes (e.g. language, working memory) in lobule VII exhibited a higher degree of convergence.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The connectivity models were generally successful in predicting cerebellar activity patterns for the new dataset.
source: As shown in Figure 5, the connectivity models were generally successful in predicting cerebellar activity patterns for the new dataset.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Ridge model provided the best overall predictive accuracy (r=0.657) in the generalization test.
source: Predictive accuracy was stable across levels of cortical granularity and the Ridge model provided the best overall predictive accuracy (r=0.657) and the WTA (r=0.352) the worst predictive accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the generalization test.

claim: The WTA model provided the worst predictive accuracy (r=0.352) in the generalization test.
source: Predictive accuracy was stable across levels of cortical granularity and the Ridge model provided the best overall predictive accuracy (r=0.657) and the WTA (r=0.352) the worst predictive accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the generalization test.

claim: Cortico-cerebellar connectivity models capture important aspects of connectivity that are stable both across tasks and participants.
source: These results provide evidence that our cortico-cerebellar connectivity models capture important aspects of connectivity that are stable both across tasks and participants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the generalization test results.

claim: Approximately 43% of the variation of cerebellar activity across tasks can be predicted by cortical activity alone.
source: Moreover, in accord with the earlier analyses based on predictions at the individual level, this generalization analysis again suggests that approximately 43% of the variation of cerebellar activity across tasks can be predicted by cortical activity alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the generalization test.

claim: Previous work on connectivity between human neocortex and cerebellum has been based on fMRI resting-state data.
source: To date, models of connectivity between the human neocortex and cerebellum have been based on fMRI resting-state data (Buckner et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2019; Marek et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buckner et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2019; and Marek et al., 2018.

claim: Each region of the cerebellum receives input from a distinct set of cortical regions.
source: This work demonstrates that each region of the cerebellum receives input from a distinct set of cortical regions.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from prior resting-state connectivity work.

claim: Anterior and posterior cerebellar motor regions show correlated activity with contralateral sensorimotor cortex.
source: For example, anterior and posterior cerebellar motor regions show correlated activity with contral-lateral sensorimotor cortex and non-motor or 'cognitive' cerebellar regions show correlated activity with specific parietal and frontal association areas.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from prior resting-state connectivity work.

claim: Non-motor or 'cognitive' cerebellar regions show correlated activity with specific parietal and frontal association areas.
source: For example, anterior and posterior cerebellar motor regions show correlated activity with contral-lateral sensorimotor cortex and non-motor or 'cognitive' cerebellar regions show correlated activity with specific parietal and frontal association areas.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from prior resting-state connectivity work.

claim: Previous work has not been designed to examine the patterns of convergence between the neocortex and cerebellum.
source: Despite these important insights, previous work has not been designed to examine the patterns of convergence between the neocortex and cerebellum.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research.

claim: Resting state connectivity maps are generally produced by assigning each cerebellar voxel to a single cortical network.
source: Resting state connectivity maps are generally produced by assigning each cerebellar voxel to a single cortical network, a de facto winner-take-all model.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in prior resting-state connectivity research.

claim: For nearly the entire cerebellum, models that allowed for some convergence predicted cerebellar activity better than the WTA model.
source: For nearly the entire cerebellum, models that allowed for some convergence predicted cerebellar activity better than the WTA model.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Regions in anterior (lobules I-V) and inferior cerebellum (lobules VIII-X) were well predicted by a relatively small and concentrated area of the neocortex.
source: Specifically, regions in anterior (lobules I-V) and inferior cerebellum (lobules VIII-X) were well predicted by a relatively small and concentrated area of the neocortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the convergence analysis.

claim: Regions in lobule VI and especially lobule VII required input from a larger and spatially more dispersed set of cortical regions.
source: In contrast, regions in lobule VI and especially lobule VII required input from a larger and spatially more dispersed set of cortical regions that were primarily located in association areas of prefrontal, parietal, and cingulate cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the convergence analysis.

claim: Cortical inputs to regions in lobule VI and VII were primarily located in association areas of prefrontal, parietal, and cingulate cortex.
source: In contrast, regions in lobule VI and especially lobule VII required input from a larger and spatially more dispersed set of cortical regions that were primarily located in association areas of prefrontal, parietal, and cingulate cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the connectivity model.

claim: The variation in convergence underscores the heterogeneity of cortico-cerebellar connectivity.
source: This finding underscores the heterogeneity of cortico-cerebellar connectivity with some cerebellar areas functioning in nearly a 1:1 relationship with a single cortical region, whereas other areas integrate input from a more diverse set of cortical regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing variation in convergence.

claim: Regions with strong convergence are anatomically restricted to lobules VI and VII.
source: Thus, rather than following a functional distinction, it appears that regions with strong convergence are anatomically restricted to lobules VI and VII, two areas that have disproportionately increased in size during primate evolution (Balsters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and citation to Balsters et al., 2010.

claim: Lobules VI and VII have disproportionately increased in size during primate evolution.

claim: A cerebellar region that forms a closed-loop circuit with a single cortical region can only fine-tune the computational processes that are ongoing in its connected cortical region.
source: A cerebellar region that forms a closed-loop circuit with a single cortical region can only fine-tune the computational processes that are ongoing in its connected cortical region.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the functional implications of one-to-one connectivity.

evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the functional implications of convergent connectivity.

claim: Pisano et al., 2021 have identified cerebellar areas that project back to multiple cortical areas in a rodent model.
source: Indeed, using a rodent model, Pisano et al., 2021 have identified cerebellar areas that project back to multiple cortical areas, providing a substrate by which the cerebellum can influence neuronal dynamics not only in a focal cortical area but also interactions within networks of cortical areas (Pisano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pisano et al., 2021.

claim: The cerebellum can influence neuronal dynamics not only in a focal cortical area but also interactions within networks of cortical areas.
source: Indeed, using a rodent model, Pisano et al., 2021 have identified cerebellar areas that project back to multiple cortical areas, providing a substrate by which the cerebellum can influence neuronal dynamics not only in a focal cortical area but also interactions within networks of cortical areas (Pisano et al., 2021).

claim: The breadth of tasks in the multi-domain task battery assured that there would be reliable variation in activity across most of the neocortex and cerebellum.
source: First, the breadth of tasks included in the battery assured that there would be reliable variation in activity across most of the neocortex and cerebellum, a necessary precondition for building a complete connectivity model.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: The dataset allowed avoidance of biases that arise from correlated noise across abutting cortical and cerebellar regions.
source: Second, the dataset allowed us to avoid biases that arise from correlated noise across abutting cortical and cerebellar regions (Buckner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological advantage of the experimental design, with citation to Buckner et al., 2011.

claim: Cortical activity patterns from one session were used to predict cerebellar activity patterns in a different session, relying on the fact that measurement noise is independent across sessions.
source: We used the cortical activity patterns from one session to predict cerebellar activity patterns in a different session, relying on the fact that measurement noise is independent across sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Resting-state correlations are predictive of task-based activation patterns.
source: While resting-state correlations are predictive of task-based activation patterns (King et al., 2019; Tavor et al., 2016; Zhi et al., 2022), resting in an fMRI scanner is arguably a relatively restricted situation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to King et al., 2019; Tavor et al., 2016; and Zhi et al., 2022.

claim: The connectivity model can robustly predict activity patterns for new tasks and participants.
source: Our generalization test shows that the connectivity model can robustly predict activity patterns for new tasks and participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the generalization test results.

claim: Increases in cerebellar blood flow are the result of increases in mossy fiber activity.
source: Increases in cerebellar blood flow, a major contributor to the BOLD signal, are the result of increases in mossy fiber activity, the primary input to the cerebellar cortex (Alahmadi et al., 2015; Alahmadi et al., 2016; Gagliano et al., 2022; Mapelli et al., 2017; Mathiesen et al., 2000; Thomsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alahmadi et al., 2015; Alahmadi et al., 2016; Gagliano et al., 2022; Mapelli et al., 2017; Mathiesen et al., 2000; and Thomsen et al., 2004.

claim: Mossy fibers are the primary input to the cerebellar cortex.
source: Increases in cerebellar blood flow, a major contributor to the BOLD signal, are the result of increases in mossy fiber activity, the primary input to the cerebellar cortex (Alahmadi et al., 2015; Alahmadi et al., 2016; Gagliano et al., 2022; Mapelli et al., 2017; Mathiesen et al., 2000; Thomsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Even a dramatic increase in the firing rate of Purkinje cells does not produce a measurable change in blood flow within the cerebellar cortex.
source: In contrast, even a dramatic increase in the (complex or simple spike) firing rate of Purkinje cells does not produce a measurable change in blood flow within the cerebellar cortex (Thomsen et al., 2004; Thomsen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thomsen et al., 2004 and Thomsen et al., 2009.

claim: The cerebellar BOLD signal provides a relatively clear image of the cortical inputs to the cerebellum.
source: Thus, the cerebellar BOLD signal provides a relatively clear image of the cortical inputs to the cerebellum; importantly, this signal does not provide information about the output of the cerebellar cortex (or cerebellum in general).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known sources of the cerebellar BOLD signal.

claim: The cerebellar BOLD signal does not provide information about the output of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Thus, the cerebellar BOLD signal provides a relatively clear image of the cortical inputs to the cerebellum; importantly, this signal does not provide information about the output of the cerebellar cortex (or cerebellum in general).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known sources of the cerebellar BOLD signal.

claim: Correlations in the fMRI signal between the neocortex and cerebellum will more strongly reflect the flow of information from the cortex to the cerebellum than the reverse.
source: Given this asymmetry, a priori, we should expect that correlations in the fMRI signal between the neocortex and cerebellum will more strongly reflect the flow of information from the cortex to the cerebellum than the reverse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential contributions to BOLD signals in the two structures.

claim: Some of the convergent inputs identified in the modeling work may be due to divergent projections from a single cerebellar region to multiple cortical regions.
source: Nonetheless, it is possible that some of the convergent inputs identified in our modeling work may be due to divergent projections from a single cerebellar region to multiple cortical regions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative interpretations of the findings.

claim: Some cerebellar areas project to the reticular nuclei in the thalamus, which in turn projects to a wide array of cortical regions.
source: Indeed, recent viral tracing work has shown that some cerebellar areas project to the reticular nuclei in the thalamus, which in turn projects to a wide array of cortical regions (Kelly and Strick, 2003; Pisano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kelly and Strick, 2003 and Pisano et al., 2021.

claim: A complete analysis of the entire cortico-cerebellar circuit will require methods such as viral tracing techniques or functional activation measures that target key nodes in the ascending pathway.
source: A complete analysis of the entire cortico-cerebellar circuit will require the methods such as viral tracing techniques (Kelly and Strick, 2003; Pisano et al., 2021) or functional activation measures that target key nodes in the ascending pathway (deep cerebellar nuclei, thalamus).
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions, with citations to Kelly and Strick, 2003 and Pisano et al., 2021.

claim: There can be substantial collinearity between different cortical regions.
source: From a statistical perspective, it was not clear, a priori, that we would have the power to distinguish between models of connectivity given that there can be substantial collinearity between different cortical regions.
evidence: This is a statement about a methodological concern, based on knowledge of cortical organization.

evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The general picture of variation in connectivity holds for both the Ridge and Lasso models.
source: Importantly, this ambiguity does not impact the core observation that the degree of convergence varies systematically across the cerebellar cortex. Whether using measures based on cortical surface area or dispersion, the general picture of variation in connectivity holds for both the Ridge and Lasso models, as well as when using cortical parcellations of different granularity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the consistency of findings across different models and parcellations.

claim: The variation in convergence reflects a stable, method-independent characteristic of the cortico-cerebellar system.
source: Thus, we are confident that the variation in convergence reflects a stable, method-independent characteristic of the cortico-cerebellar system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the consistency of findings across different methods.

claim: The connectivity model was able to take cortical activity patterns to make fairly accurate predictions of cerebellar activity, even when the data were obtained in a completely separate experiment.
source: The connectivity model was able to take cortical activity patterns to make fairly accurate predictions of cerebellar activity, even when the data were obtained in a completely separate experiment from that used to build the model.

claim: A substantial proportion of the cortico-cerebellar communication can be described by fixed information flow.
source: This finding suggests that a substantial proportion of the cortico-cerebellar communication can be described by fixed information flow (Cole et al., 2016); that is, each area of the cerebellum simply receives, independent of task, a copy of the neural activity occurring in the corresponding cortical areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on the generalization test results, with citation to Cole et al., 2016.

claim: Each area of the cerebellum simply receives, independent of task, a copy of the neural activity occurring in the corresponding cortical areas.
